rag.name: Submodule.iSup_smul
rag.content:
theorem iSup_smul {ι : Sort*} {t : ι → Submodule R A} {N : Submodule R M} :
    (⨆ i, t i) • N = ⨆ i, t i • N :=
  le_antisymm (smul_le.mpr fun t ht s hs ↦ iSup_induction _ (C := (· • s ∈ _)) ht
    (fun i t ht ↦ mem_iSup_of_mem i <| smul_mem_smul ht hs)
    (by simp_rw [zero_smul]; apply zero_mem) fun x y ↦ by simp_rw [add_smul]; apply add_mem)
    (iSup_le fun i ↦ Submodule.smul_mono_left <| le_iSup _ i)

namespace Subrepresentation

open Pointwise

universe u

variable {A : Type*} [CommRing A] {G : Type*} [Group G] {W : Type*} [AddCommMonoid W] [Module A W]
  {ρ : Representation A G W}
informal_statement: For any two subrepresentations \( \rho_1 \) and \( \rho_2 \), the infimum of \( \rho_1 \) and \( \rho_2 \) when converted to submodules is equal to the infimum of the submodules corresponding to \( \rho_1 \) and \( \rho_2 \).
informal_proof: The equality follows directly from the definitions involved, as both sides represent the infimum of the corresponding submodules. Therefore, the proof is trivially true by reflexivity.

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
C1_dependencies.compilationAlias:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
